unit.title: Edo and the floating world
unit.question: How did a city turn pictures into a mass market, and who got named when it did?

shots.text: Edo, 1603–1868. A city of over a million learned to sell pictures for the price of a bowl of noodles.
shots.alt: Washi paper. The characters 浮世, the floating world, bleed into it like ink.

shots.text: Around 1831 a publisher bet a series on an imported blue. Hokusai, past seventy, gave him this wave.
shots.alt: Hokusai’s Great Wave, separated into five layers of depth: sky, far swell, near swell, the wave, the foam.

shots.text: Prints were products: planned, paid for and sold from shops like this one, drawn by Hokusai in 1802.
shots.alt: Hokusai’s picture of a print shop, sheets hanging at the front and books piled on the floor.

shots.text: One sheet, many hands: a designer drew it, a carver cut the blocks, a printer pulled each colour.
shots.alt: The Wave’s colour layers, a reconstruction, dropping one by one onto the registration marks.

shots.text: Publishers clustered in Edo’s centre. Their prints followed the Tōkaidō, the lords’ road to Kyoto.

shots.text: From 1790 every design needed a censor’s seal. In 1842 the state banned the trade’s two best sellers.

beats.text:
On 3 July 2024 Japan issued a new thousand-yen note. On its back is this wave, caught just before it breaks, with Mount Fuji small behind it.
The picture was printed in Edo around 1831. It sold for about the price of a bowl of noodles.
Eleven years later, the state that now prints it on money banned half of what the trade sold, and capped the price of the rest.

This unit asks one question. **How did a city turn pictures into a mass market, and who got named when it did?**
You will follow five publishers’ bets, one to an act, and one sheet of paper from Echizen to New York.
The map and the timeline move as you read. Every person you meet joins the Cast, bottom left.

acts.title: The quarter’s publisher
acts.bet: A publisher born in the pleasure quarter bets that a city of a million will pay for its glamour, and answers a fine with luxury.

segments.title: A city built to be an audience

beats.text:
In 1603 [[ieyasu]] became shogun and made Edo, a castle town on a marshy bay, the seat of his government.
The emperor stayed in Kyoto. Osaka stayed the country’s warehouse.
From 1635 every lord in Japan had to live in Edo in alternate years, leaving his wife and heir behind when he went home.
Their processions filled the roads. Their households filled the city.

In the first month of 1657 a fire broke out at Honmyō-ji temple in Hongō, at about two in the afternoon.
The next morning a second fire started in Koishikawa. That afternoon a third began in Kōjimachi.
Between sixty and seventy per cent of the city burned, and the castle keep was never rebuilt.
The dead are counted at anything from thirty thousand to a hundred thousand.

The rebuilt city spread east. A bridge at Ryōgoku crossed the Sumida, and the districts of Honjo and Fukagawa grew on the far bank.
The fire also moved the licensed quarter. It had stood near Nihonbashi since 1617.
After 1657 it was rebuilt in the rice fields north of Asakusa, behind a moat with a single gate, as the Shin-Yoshiwara.

figure.cap: Picture book of play synopses for the Nakamura theatre, dated 1799 · Torii-school artist · The Met 2013.851 · CC0

guess.q: In 1721 Edo counted itself. About how many people lived there?
guess.say: About 1.3 million by the city’s own count, samurai and townspeople in nearly equal numbers. The buyers came before the pictures.

beats.text:
Edo’s leisure ran through two licensed businesses. Three kabuki theatres stood in the town centre, at Sakai-chō, Fukiya-chō and Kobiki-chō.
The quarter stood at the edge.
Both sold glamour to a city with time and money, and both needed advertising.
Because the state licensed them, it could later ban them by name.

In 1721 the shogunate counted the city. Edo held about 1.3 million people, samurai and townspeople in nearly equal numbers.
It was among the largest cities anywhere.
Half the city served the lords who came and went. The other half fed, clothed and amused them.
A market for cheap pictures needed exactly this: crowds, cash and visitors who wanted to take something home.

Pictures had been printed from woodblocks in Japan for centuries, mostly Buddhist images and book illustrations.
In the 1670s Edo began trading pictures as goods. [[moronobu]] signed his book pictures from 1672, and the earliest known single sheets follow.
The trade called its subject *ukiyo*, the floating world: once a Buddhist word for a sorrowful world, now the world of passing pleasures.

The earliest known *uki-e*, “floating pictures”, date from about 1739–40.
They used one-point perspective, learned from European engravings that reached Japan through Dejima or China.
Designers favoured interiors, because perspective is easier to apply to architecture than to landscape.
In 1748 [[masanobu]] drew a whole kabuki theatre, crowd and stage, running towards one vanishing point.

A print was never one hand. The **publisher** planned it, paid for it, applied for permission and sold it.
The **designer** drew it on thin paper. The **carver** pasted that drawing face down on cherry wood and cut through it, destroying it.
The **printer** inked the blocks and rubbed each sheet by hand.
This is a carver’s key block, pulled in black. The notches outside the picture registered every colour block that followed.

Full colour arrived in a single year, and not from the trade.
For New Year 1765, circles of amateur poets commissioned picture calendars to exchange at parties. They paid for the best designers, carvers and paper.
Publishers then bought the blocks, cut out the patrons’ names and sold the sheets as *nishiki-e*, brocade pictures (probable).
The poets’ favourite designer was [[harunobu]]. He had five years left to live.

[[tsutaya]] was born in the Shin-Yoshiwara in 1750 and grew up there.
His first business was a bookshop on the road to the quarter’s gate. His first product was its printed guide, the *Yoshiwara saiken*, which he came to publish alone.
In 1783 he moved into the city, to Tōri Abura-chō by Nihonbashi, the street of the big houses.
His seal was an ivy leaf under a three-peaked Fuji.

This is what a print shop looked like, drawn by Hokusai for a picture book of 1802. The Tokyo Metropolitan Library identifies it as Tsutaya’s own shop (probable).
Sheets hang in the front, books lie in piles.
Publishers sold from their shops, swapped stock with each other and supplied street sellers.
Some 655 lending libraries carried books door to door in 1808.

figure.cap: Utagawa Hiroshige, Cherry Blossom Time in Nakanochō, the quarter’s main street · LACMA via Wikimedia Commons · public domain

beats.text:
The quarter’s women were there under contract. A typical indenture around 1800, signed by a father, exchanged a lump sum for years of service: for instance 25 ryō for five.
Debts for food, clothes and medicine could extend the term.
From 1793 the only women prints could name were courtesans. [[hanaogi]] wrote poetry admired in her day. In 1794 she ran away, and was brought back.

guess.q: From 1790, whose marks on this sheet made them answerable to the law?
guess.say: The designer’s signature and the publisher’s mark. The law named designer, writer and publisher; the carver and the printer appear nowhere on the sheet.

beats.text:
In 1787 [[sadanobu]] became chief councillor and began the Kansei reforms, after years of famine and spending.
From the fifth month of 1790 publishers had to submit every design to censors chosen from their own guild.
Approval was a small round seal reading *kiwame*, “examined”, cut into the key block.
On this Utamaro, Tsutaya’s ivy leaf and the censor’s seal sit side by side.

The law named three people for every sheet: the designer, the writer and the publisher. It never named the carver or the printer.
It came with examples. In 1791 three of Kyōden’s books, published by Tsutaya, were judged offensive.
[[kyoden]] was manacled for fifty days. Tsutaya was fined half of everything he owned.
From 1800 large bust portraits of women were banned as “conspicuous”.

Tsutaya answered the fine with luxury. [[utamaro]]’s bust portraits of women on powdered mica were the luxury prints of the decade.
Then, in the fifth month of 1794, he issued actor portraits by an unknown designer signed [[sharaku]].
About 140 designs followed in ten months, all for Tsutaya. Then nothing.
Nobody knows who Sharaku was.

Osaka ran the same medium another way.
In the eighth month of 1793 the publisher [[shioya]] won the sole right to publish actor likenesses. In 1794 he bought a rival artist’s blocks.
That artist, [[ryukosai]], “never put his signature” on the prints Shioya made from his designs, and withdrew.
In Osaka, fan clubs and poetry circles paid for much of the trade.

Tsutaya died in 1797, aged 47. His shop went on under his name.
In 1804 Utamaro was manacled for fifty days for a print of the warlord Hideyoshi, a subject the state treated as its own. He died two years later.
The golden age ended in handcuffs twice.
The censor now held the publisher answerable for every sheet. What would a publisher dare to bet on next?

acts.title: A bet on blue
acts.bet: A publisher bets a landscape series on a cheap imported blue, and an old designer gives it the sheet the world remembers.

segments.title: The old man and the pigment

beats.text:
[[hokusai]] was born in Edo in 1760. Between 16 and 19 he trained to cut woodblocks.
He then studied under the actor-print designer [[shunsho]], signing himself Shunrō, and Tsutaya published some of his early work.
In 1807 Edo’s picture publishers formed a guild, the *jihon toiya*, which owned the blocks and policed copying.
Hokusai would be over seventy before his most famous sheet.

In 1814 a Nagoya publisher, [[eirakuya]], began issuing the *Hokusai Manga*. These were sketchbooks of people, animals, gods and things, sold as models for amateurs.
This copy of the first volume is a later printing, after 1828.
The books made Hokusai a brand outside Edo. Whether they make him the “father of manga” is still a question, even in a British Museum curator’s title.

guess.q: Where was the new blue first made? Tap the map.
guess.say: Berlin, around 1704. By the 1820s Chinese supply made it cheap (probable that it was made there). It was never made in Japan in this period.

beats.text:
The Fuji series would be sold on a colour Edo could not make.
Printers already had indigo from plants, but it printed dull and was hard to grade into a sky.
The new blue was a chemical pigment, bright and steady, and it came from very far away.
It reached Japan the only way foreign goods could: through the port of Nagasaki.

Prussian blue was first made in Berlin around 1704, by accident: a colour-maker’s red came out blue.
Edo called it *bero-ai*, “Berlin indigo”.
Dutch ships brought it to Nagasaki via the Cape and Batavia.
Then, from 1824, Chinese junks re-entered the trade “in steadily increasing quantities”, and the price began to fall.

argued.q: When did Prussian blue reach Edo’s printers?

a.title: Around 1790
a.text: One reading has it arriving through Dejima around 1790 and staying costly until about 1820.

b.title: In the late 1820s
b.text: Another has it known but little used until Chinese imports from 1824 made it cheap enough for a sixteen-mon sheet.

evidence.t: The Dutch withdraw from the blue trade

argued.why: The price fall is what turned a luxury into a print colour. It supports the later date for printers, without denying earlier arrivals.

beats.text:
Historians agree the blue came by sea. They disagree about when Edo’s printers could afford it.
The line on the timeline is Henry Smith’s figure for the Chinese price at Nagasaki, from 87 to 31 monme of silver a kin.
Read both positions, then decide which the price supports.

In 1829 the fan-maker [[iseya]] put out a fan by [[eisen]] printed in light and dark shades of the new blue alone.
By the bookseller [[toho]]’s account it was a sensation, and other fan-makers flooded the market with all-blue fans.
This Eisen sheet, from the early 1830s, is printed the same way: one imported colour, in gradations, on white paper.

Then, Tōho says, [[nishimuraya]] of Bakuro-chō issued Hokusai’s *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji* in the new blue. It was “a great fad, double that of the fans.”
His advertisement, printed for New Year 1831, promised one view to a sheet and “more than one hundred, without being limited to thirty-six”.
Thirty-six became forty-six. This is Red Fuji, one of the earliest.

This scene begins inside the wave. Look at the hollow under the claw, where three boats lie low in the water.
That blue was new in 1831. It is the reason this sheet exists.
Before it was a picture of anything, it was a product: a publisher’s bet, a pigment’s price and a workshop’s labour.

guess.q: What did Hokusai draw rising over the boats?
guess.say: A plunging storm wave, about ten metres high and about three kilometres offshore. A tsunami travels low out at sea.

beats.text:
The title places the scene “off Kanagawa”, a post station on the bay road south of Edo. Fuji stands about eighty kilometres west.
Three long boats ride a swell, their crews bent at the oars.
The sea has been read many ways since. Scientists have measured it against what real water does.

labels.yokohama-off: Storm wave · c. 10 m · c. 3 km out

beats.text:
Two scientists who studied the picture concluded Hokusai drew “an exceptionally large storm wave”, not a tsunami.
A tsunami travels low and fast out at sea, and rises only near the shore.
Another team put this wave near ten metres high, about three kilometres offshore.
The drawing is exaggerated, and still faithful to water.

The Met examined its Great Waves with a spectrometer.
The dark stripes of the wave mix the new Prussian blue with old indigo.
The deep hollow is pure Prussian blue, printed twice.
Those are decisions about blocks and ink, made in a workshop. The sheet credits one man: 北斎改為一筆, “Hokusai, changing his name to Iitsu, drew this.”

links.label: Print it yourself in the Workshop

beats.text:
Here the Met’s image is separated by colour, one layer per ink. Lay them down in order.
A real edition needed a block for each colour, cut by hand and registered to the notches.
One printer could pull about two hundred sheets a day. A publisher needed to sell about two thousand to profit.

There is no single Great Wave. There is an edition, pulled from the same blocks over months or years as the wood wore down.
By 2020 the British Museum had located 111 impressions; by 2024, 113.
No block survives. The most quoted estimate, up to 8,000 sheets, is an inference from wear (argued).
Compare three originals under the loupe.

a.title: Hokusai
a.text: The design is one man’s, made at seventy after fifty years of drawing. In 1834 he wrote that by 110 every dot and line would live.

b.title: A system
b.text: A publisher’s bet, a pigment’s price, a carver who cut the foam and a printer who pulled the blue twice. Only one is named.

evidence.t: The hollow was printed twice in pure Prussian blue

argued.why: Mostly B: double printing was the printer’s work, even if the designer asked for it. The sheet shows a team; the signature shows one name.

beats.text:
Two readings of authorship meet in this sheet. One is the genius in the signature. The other is the trade that made it.
Hokusai’s own workshop complicates both: his daughter [[oi]] painted inside it.
Weigh the evidence, then choose.

This night scene in the Yoshiwara is by Katsushika Ōi. Only about ten works are confirmed as hers.
Hokusai “is reported to have said” her pictures of women were better than his.
Orders sent to “Hokusai” could be painted by father or daughter and signed with his name (probable).
One historian argues her hand was made to vanish, “for profit”.

Hokusai knew whose hands mattered.
In 1835 he wanted a particular carver, [[egawa]], for his *One Hundred Views of Mount Fuji*. To get him, he offered to give up his own share of the carving fee.
The letter implies designers normally took a cut of the carver’s pay for bringing the work.
It is one of very few records of what a carver was worth.

In 1833–34 [[hiroshige]] designed the *Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō* for the publisher [[hoeido]]: fifty-five sheets from Nihonbashi to Kyoto.
The Tōkaidō was the lords’ road between the two capitals.
Some sheets were reprinted twelve to fifteen thousand times, by the usual estimate.
Watch the road draw itself, station by station.

acts.title: The ban and the hundred views
acts.bet: The state bans the trade’s two best sellers and caps the rest. Publishers bet on warriors, cats and a hundred views of the city.

beats.text:
A record of 1805 prices an ordinary sheet at twenty mon. A bowl of *kake-soba* cost sixteen.
A picture cost about a meal, which is what made it a mass product.
In 1841 [[tadakuni]] began the Tenpō reforms, a second attempt to discipline the city’s spending.
The price lane on the timeline is about to change.

guess.q: An ordinary ten-colour sheet sold for about 24 mon. What ceiling did the state set?
guess.say: Sixteen mon, the price of one bowl of soba: a cut of about a third, ordered in the eleventh month of 1842.

beats.text:
In the sixth month of 1842 the town order reached the prints.
「錦絵と唱、歌舞伎役者遊女女芸者等を壱枚摺ニ致候義、風俗ニ拘り候筋ニ付」
Single sheets of kabuki actors, courtesans and geisha “concern public morals”. Their publication, and the sale of existing stock, were forbidden.
Subjects should be loyalty, filial piety, chastity and children’s moral instruction.

In the eleventh month came the price.
「壱枚絵団扇絵共、拾六文以上は無用之事」: single sheets and fan prints, nothing above sixteen mon.
Printings were limited to seven or eight, and sets to three sheets (probable).
An ordinary ten-colour sheet had sold for about twenty-four. The state had banned the trade’s two best sellers and cut the price of the rest by a third.

figure.cap: Utagawa Kunisada, the actor Ichikawa Danjūrō VII, 1826 · Art Institute of Chicago 1937.270 · CC0

beats.text:
The three theatres were ordered out of the city centre to a new street, Saruwaka-chō, near the road to the Yoshiwara.
The state put its licensed pleasures together, at the edge.
[[danjuro]], the most famous actor in Japan, was banished from Edo for extravagance (probable).
Watch the theatres move.

links.label: Date prints on the Seal Timeline

beats.text:
The censor’s machine changed with the subjects.
From 1843 ward headmen, *nanushi*, stamped prints with their own names: one seal, then two from 1847, then two with a date.
From 1853 a single seal reading *aratame*, “examined”, usually came with a date seal.
So a sheet’s margin dates it to within a few years. Remember the four bands.

The ban made warriors the safest genre, and [[kuniyoshi]] had drawn them since 1827.
In 1847 he gave the trade the loyal retainers of the forty-seven rōnin, one to a sheet, fifty-one in all. The censor [[murata]] approved them.
The [[fujiokaya]] records how many sets sold between the seventh month of 1847 and the third of 1848.
The same diary records a flop.

argued.q: Did the ban create the landscape print?

a.title: Yes
a.text: With actors and beauties forbidden, views of famous places became the safe product, and the trade poured into them.

b.title: No: it sped it up
b.text: The Fuji series was out in 1831 and the Tōkaidō in 1833. The ban protected a genre already selling, and pushed the trade towards warriors.

evidence.t: 1847: six or seven tenths of sales were actor pictures “without names”

argued.why: The trade routed around the ban with disguised actors, not mainly with landscapes, which were already a market.

beats.text:
A common story says the ban made the landscape print.
The dates on the timeline complicate it, and so does what a magistrate found when he counted the shops five years later.
Weigh the two readings.

The edict named actors, courtesans and geisha. It did not name ghosts, monsters or cats.
Kuniyoshi drew all three. This is the monster cat of Okazaki, from a ghost play set on the Tōkaidō: a cat, a play and an actor’s face at once.
The ban sharpened the trade’s talent for saying one thing with another.

segments.title: A hundred views of a city about to be renamed

beats.text:
In 1852 the United States sent a naval squadron to open Japan’s ports to its ships.
Its commander was Commodore [[perry]], who carried a letter from the president to the shogun.
Edo’s trade knew nothing of it yet. Its shops were selling warriors, views and cats.
The squadron would take eight months to arrive.

guess.q: Perry sailed from Virginia to Edo Bay. Which way round did he go?

options.label: West: round South America, across the Pacific
East: round Africa, through the Indian Ocean

guess.say: East: Madeira, the Cape, Mauritius, Ceylon, Singapore and China. Eight months to Uraga.

beats.text:
The squadron left Hampton Roads, Virginia, on 24 November 1852.
Edo Bay lay on the far side of the world, by either ocean.
A steamship needed coal every few weeks, so the route was a chain of ports where coal could be bought or stored.
The map shows only the start and the end.

Perry crossed the Atlantic to Madeira, rounded the Cape of Good Hope, called at Mauritius, Ceylon and Singapore, and gathered his ships in China.
On 8 July 1853 four American ships anchored off Uraga, at the mouth of Edo Bay.
A treaty followed in 1854.
The trade that had grown up behind closed ports was about to meet the world.

On 11 November 1855 an earthquake struck Edo, and thousands died.
Within two days the shops were selling *namazu-e*, pictures of the giant catfish said to cause earthquakes. One study counts about 380 kinds (probable).
Most were unsigned and uncensored. Here the god of Kashima pins the catfish with his sword.
The trade moved at the speed of news.

Between 1856 and 1858 Hiroshige designed the *One Hundred Famous Views of Edo* for the publisher [[uoya]]. There are 118 views, with a title page by another hand.
Every view stood somewhere you could walk to. Each dot on this map of 1859 is one of them, coloured by season.
Tap any dot to see the sheet. Hiroshige died in 1858, as the set was being finished.

This is one of the hundred views: a sudden shower over the Shin-Ōhashi bridge, 1857.
Everything the sheet says about its own making sits outside the picture.
Follow a curator through its five marks, in the order a curator reads them. The seals alone will date the sheet.

figure.cap: Utagawa Yoshikazu, Americans Baking Bread, 1861 · Art Institute of Chicago 1926.1692 · CC0

beats.text:
In 1859 a fishing village on the Kanagawa shore, close to where Hokusai set his wave, became the treaty port of Yokohama.
Foreign merchants, ships and households arrived.
Within a year or two Edo’s publishers were selling *Yokohama-e*, prints of the newcomers at work and at home.
It was the last new genre the Edo trade invented.

In 1864 synthetic aniline dyes arrived, and the palette of the last prints turned to hard reds and purples.
In 1868 the shogunate fell, the emperor moved to Edo, and the city was renamed Tokyo.
In 1872 a decree cancelled the debts of the Yoshiwara’s women (probable).
The trade did not end. It was about to find its best customers.

acts.title: The second trade
acts.kicker: Act IV · 1865–1928 · Hayashi, Bing and Wright
acts.bet: Dealers bet that the cheap sheets of a closed city will sell as art abroad, and the buyers start to write the history.

beats.text:
In 1867 Japan sent an official exhibit to the Paris exposition. It was the shogunate’s last year of rule.
Visitors saw prints, books, lacquer and porcelain side by side, sent by the state that had once censored the prints.
Paris already had shops selling Japanese goods (probable).
How Europe had met the prints in the first place became a story of its own.

guess.q: A famous story says Europe found ukiyo-e as packing paper. When was it first printed?
guess.say: In 1905, in a memoir, half a century after the 1856 it describes. It speaks of one bound book, not wrapping paper.

beats.text:
In 1865 French mail steamers opened a branch line to Yokohama.
After the Suez Canal opened in 1869, the Messageries Maritimes ran through-sailings from Marseille to Yokohama, from April 1870.
Prints, books, lacquer and porcelain now had a regular road to Europe.
Every crate that reached Paris carried its own small story of arrival, and some of those stories grew in the telling.

The packing-paper story’s earliest printed source is a memoir of 1905.
At the printer Delâtre’s, the engraver Bracquemond found “un petit livre bizarrement broché”, a small oddly bound book, wedging porcelain.
It was a volume of the Manga, not loose sheets, and its date of 1856 is disputed.
Retellings turned it into wrapping paper.

[[hayashi]] came to Paris as an interpreter for the exposition of 1878 and opened a shop in 1884.
Over eleven years he made 218 shipments from Japan.
One count gives 166,000 prints and 9,708 illustrated books. Another says more than 300,000 works (argued).
The second trade had a Japanese dealer at its centre.

[[bing]], a Hamburg-born dealer in Paris, published *Le Japon artistique* from 1888 to 1891: thirty-six issues in French, English and German.
In 1890 he hung over seven hundred prints at the École des Beaux-Arts.
His shop would later give a name to Art Nouveau.
The painters came to look.

[[vangogh]] bought about 660 Japanese prints in early 1887 and hung some in a Paris café.
That autumn he painted three copies in oil. Two were after Hiroshige: a plum orchard, and the sudden shower over Shin-Ōhashi. The third copied a courtesan by Eisen.
The copies are in Amsterdam. The museum’s licence is non-commercial, so they are linked, not shown.

a.title: Exchange
a.text: Japan showed itself at Paris on purpose, Japanese dealers chose and sold the prints, and European art changed for good.

b.title: Appropriation
b.text: Europe took the forms without the makers, prized single sheets as curios, and named the borrowing after itself: Japonisme.

evidence.t: Hayashi chose and shipped much of what Paris saw
Japan exhibited at Paris in 1867 and 1878

argued.why: Mostly A for this evidence: the selection was Japanese. The B reading still holds for how the prints were displayed and credited.

beats.text:
The borrowing has a name, *Japonisme*, and a counter-name, appropriation.
Both describe something real.
Weigh one piece of evidence against the two readings.

From 1 January 1867 Pacific Mail steamers ran from San Francisco to Yokohama. From 1869 a railroad crossed America.
Boston bought first and most. Its Museum of Fine Arts now holds more than forty-five thousand Japanese prints.
American collectors became the second trade’s other great market.
Some of them went to Japan to buy at the source.

guess.q: In 1898 Tokyo saw its earliest known exhibition of ukiyo-e. Who curated it?
guess.say: Ernest Fenollosa, Boston’s curator of Japanese art. Japan’s own show of its popular prints was organised by an American.

beats.text:
At home the prints were still cheap goods, sold by the sheet and pasted on walls.
Japan’s art schools and museums of the 1880s were built around painting, sculpture and temple treasures.
The idea that a sixteen-mon sheet belonged in an exhibition came slowly, and partly from outside.
The timeline’s afterlife lane is filling up.

[[fenollosa]] came to Japan in 1878 to teach philosophy and political economy at the Imperial University in Tokyo.
He helped found the Tokyo School of Fine Arts, then became curator of Oriental art at Boston’s Museum of Fine Arts in 1890.
In 1898 he curated an exhibition of ukiyo-e in Tokyo: the earliest known in Japan.

[[wright]] first went to Japan in 1905. In 1906 he lent the Art Institute of Chicago a whole exhibition of Hiroshige.
He dealt in prints for twenty years. A deal with the Spauldings in 1913 grew from twenty thousand dollars to 125,000 in five months.
This Plum Garden at Kameido names him in its provenance: sold to Kate Buckingham, February 1915.

In 1919–20 some prints Wright had sold proved “revamped”: faded impressions recut and recoloured, with pinholes where new blocks were registered.
The fraud was traced to a Tokyo dealer and a collector, and cost Wright about thirty thousand dollars in refunds.
In 1928 his bank seized his house. Thousands of his prints sold at a dollar each.

In 1921 the brothers William and John Spaulding gave Boston’s Museum of Fine Arts more than six thousand prints. Their one condition was that the prints never be exhibited.
They may be studied, and never shown.
Light fades the colours that made them famous.
The afterlife had licence rules of its own.

In 1889 [[tokuno]], head of Japan’s government Printing Bureau, sent the Smithsonian a complete printing set. It held blocks, tools, pigments and over a hundred progressive proofs.
Its records name the carver [[kido]] and the printers [[yamamoto]] and [[nakamura]].
A century of nameless carvers and printers got names only when the state sent the trade abroad.

acts.bet: A central bank bets that one sixteen-mon sheet can stand for a country, and puts it on money.

beats.text:
Follow one sheet. Its paper was probably *hōsho* of paper-mulberry, the kind Echizen was famous for.
It was cut, inked and printed in Edo for Eijudō of Bakuro-chō, about 1831, and sold for sixteen to twenty mon.
How it crossed the Pacific is not recorded. In 1929 it entered the Met in the Havemeyer bequest, as JP1847.

guess.q: How many original impressions of the Great Wave are known today?
guess.say: 113 located by 2024. Up to 8,000 is an estimate of how many were printed; nobody recorded the run.

beats.text:
The JP1847 sheet is one of many pulled from the same blocks.
The runs lane shows the estimates: up to eight thousand Great Waves printed, an inference from wear in the blocks.
Paper burns, fades, tears and gets pasted to walls. Museums have spent decades counting the survivors, sheet by sheet.

The census goes on. By 2020 the British Museum had located 111 Great Waves, in eight states; by 2024, 113. Red Fuji has 93 known impressions in five.
The Met holds all forty-six Fuji designs, in 121 impressions.
None of the blocks survives, and no record of the print run exists.
Every count is a museum’s, not a publisher’s.

On 3 July 2024 the Bank of Japan put the wave on the back of the thousand-yen note.
The note’s image is not openly licensed, so it is described here, not shown.
A publisher bet this sheet on a pigment fad. A censor stamped it, and a later state capped its price. Now the state prints it as money.

Five bets. Tsutaya answered a fine with luxury. Eijudō bet on a pigment’s price. The ban turned the trade to warriors and views.
Hayashi, Bing and Wright made a second trade abroad. The Bank of Japan made an icon.
The designers were named on every sheet. The carvers and printers were named once, in 1889, for export.

tsutaya.name: Tsutaya Jūzaburō
tsutaya.cap: Santō Kyōden, caricature of Tsutaya, 1791 · National Diet Library via Wikimedia Commons · public domain (PD-Japan)
tsutaya.line: Born in the Yoshiwara. Publisher of Utamaro, Kyōden and every Sharaku. Fined half of everything he owned in 1791.
tsutaya.bet: That the city would pay for the glamour of the quarter he grew up in.

highlights.t: Published the Yoshiwara guide alone from 1776
Published Utamaro, Kyōden and every Sharaku
Fined half of everything he owned, 1791

tsutaya.story:
Tsutaya Jūzaburō was born in the Yoshiwara on 13 February 1750 and adopted into the Kitagawa family. “Tsutaya”, Ivy Shop, was a shop name, not a surname.
In 1774 he opened a bookshop on the Gojikken road to the quarter’s gate. His first books were guides to the pleasure quarter. From 1776 he published the *Yoshiwara saiken* alone.
In 1783 he moved into the city, to Tōri Abura-chō. He widened his list: comic poetry, picture books, and the writers and designers who sold them. Utamaro lived in his house from about 1783 (probable).
The Kansei reforms caught him in 1791. Kyōden was manacled and Tsutaya was fined half his property. He answered with luxury: Utamaro’s mica portraits, then, in 1794, Sharaku’s ten months of actors.
He died in 1797, aged 47; some sources say of beriberi. His shop kept his name.

nishimuraya.name: Nishimuraya Yohachi (Eijudō)
nishimuraya.line: The Eijudō firm at Bakuro-chō. Published Hokusai’s Thirty-six Views in the new blue, 1831.
nishimuraya.bet: That a series of landscapes would sell on a new blue.

highlights.t: Issued the Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji from 1831
Advertised “more than one hundred” views

nishimuraya.story:
Nishimuraya Yohachi ran the Eijudō publishing house in Bakuro-chō. Several generations used the name, so the dates on this card are approximate (probable).
Eijudō published Hokusai’s *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji*. By the bookseller Tōho’s account, he issued it in the new Prussian blue after an all-blue fan by Eisen had started a fad in 1829.
The series was, Tōho wrote, “a great fad, double that of the fans.”
His advertisement, printed for New Year 1831, promised one view to a sheet and “more than one hundred, without being limited to thirty-six”. He stopped at forty-six.
That was the bet: a cheap imported colour, a famous mountain, and a designer past seventy. The Great Wave was one sheet of it, and so was Red Fuji.
No likeness of him is known, so his card carries his firm’s name in a seal frame.

iseya.line: Fan-maker. Put out Keisai Eisen’s all-blue fan in 1829 and started the fad, by Tōho’s account.

uoya.bet: That a hundred views of one city would sell, sheet by sheet, for years.

highlights.t: Published the One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1856–58
His mark reads 下谷 魚栄, Shitaya, Uoei
Each sheet carries aratame and a date seal

uoya.story:
Uoya Eikichi was a publisher in Shitaya, in the north of the city. His mark on the margin reads 下谷 魚栄, Shitaya, Uoei.
Almost everything known about him comes from the sheets he paid for. Between 1856 and 1858 he issued Hiroshige’s *One Hundred Famous Views of Edo*: 118 views, and a title page by another hand.
It was a bet on scale. Each sheet needed its own blocks, carvers and printers, and its own approval: an *aratame* seal and a seal giving the year and month.
Those seals now date the series sheet by sheet. *Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi* carries 巳九, the ninth month of the Snake year, 1857.
Hiroshige died in 1858, while the set was being finished. The series outlived them both. Van Gogh copied two of its sheets in Paris in 1887.
No likeness of Uoya is known, so his card carries his mark.

eirakuya.line: A Nagoya house. Published the Hokusai Manga from 1814.

shioya.line: Osaka. Granted the sole right to publish actor likenesses in the 8th month of 1793.

moronobu.line: Signed his book pictures from 1672. The earliest known single-sheet prints follow.

masanobu.line: Edo designer of perspective prints. His kabuki theatre of 1748, an uki-e, is in the Met.

harunobu.line: The designer the poetry circles chose for the full-colour calendars of 1765. No likeness of him survives.

shunsho.name: Katsukawa Shunshō
shunsho.line: Actors with recognisable faces. Hokusai’s first teacher.

utamaro.cap: Portrait attributed to Chōbunsai Eishi, 1815 · British Museum via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
utamaro.line: Bust portraits of women for Tsutaya in the 1790s. Manacled for fifty days in 1804; dead in 1806.
utamaro.bet: That a face, close up, could sell a sheet.

highlights.t: Bust portraits of women for Tsutaya, 1790s
More than 2,000 known prints
Manacled fifty days in 1804

utamaro.story:
Little is known of Kitagawa Utamaro’s early life. His birthplace is given as Kyoto, Osaka, Edo or Kawagoe, and none is verified. As a boy he studied with the painter Toriyama Sekien.
In the mid-1780s, probably 1783, he went to live with Tsutaya Jūzaburō. The partnership made him.
In the 1790s he designed *ōkubi-e*, large-headed pictures of beautiful women, often on a glittering ground of powdered mica.
The censors pursued the genre. From 1793 prints could name no women but courtesans, and from 1800 large bust portraits of women were banned.
In 1804 he was manacled for fifty days for prints of the warlord Toyotomi Hideyoshi, a forbidden subject. He died on 31 October 1806.
More than two thousand of his prints are known. He was one of few ukiyo-e designers famous across Japan in his lifetime.

sharaku.name: Tōshūsai Sharaku
sharaku.line: About 140 actor prints in ten months of 1794–95, all published by Tsutaya. Identity unknown.
sharaku.bet: That a buyer wanted the actor’s real face, not an ideal one.

highlights.t: About 144 actor portraits in ten months
Every one published by Tsutaya
Identity: no theory widely accepted

sharaku.story:
Tōshūsai Sharaku appears in the fifth month of 1794 and is gone by the first month of 1795. Neither his real name nor his dates are known; the bar on the timeline marks only his working months.
In those ten months Tsutaya published about 144 of his portraits of kabuki actors, which historians divide into four periods.
The first, large heads on a dark mica ground, survive in the most copies, which suggests they sold best. Many later designs survive in a single copy.
His actors are not flattered. Contemporaries such as Utamaro idealised their subjects; Sharaku showed the jowls and the strain. Then the work stopped.
Dozens of identities have been proposed: an obscure poet, the Noh actor Saitō Jūrōbei, even Hokusai. Few are taken seriously, and none is widely accepted.
His fame came late: he was rarely mentioned in print until Julius Kurth’s book of 1910.

ryukosai.name: Ryūkōsai Jokei
ryukosai.line: Osaka. Never signed the prints Shioya published from his designs, and withdrew.

hokusai.name: Katsushika Hokusai
hokusai.cap: Keisai Eisen, portrait of Hokusai · Wikimedia Commons · public domain (PD-Japan)
hokusai.line: Trained to cut woodblocks between 16 and 19. The Manga from 1814; the Fuji series from 1831.
hokusai.bet: That a lifetime of drawing could still be improving at ninety.

highlights.t: Trained as a block-cutter, aged 16–19
Known by at least thirty names
Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji, c. 1830–32

hokusai.story:
Katsushika Hokusai was born in Edo in 1760. As a teenager he trained to cut woodblocks, then entered the studio of the actor-print designer Katsushika Shunshō.
He used at least thirty names in his life, changing them as his work changed. The Great Wave is signed with one of them, Iitsu.
His *Manga* sketchbooks began in 1814. The *Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji*, for Eijudō, followed around 1830–32, when he was past seventy.
He knew the trade’s other hands. In 1835 he gave up his share of a carving fee to secure the carver Egawa Tomekichi.
In 1834 he wrote that at a hundred and ten “each dot, each line will possess a life of its own”. He died on 10 May 1849, reportedly asking for five more years.
His output is put at more than thirty thousand paintings, sketches, prints and book pictures. His daughter Ōi painted beside him.

oi.name: Katsushika Ōi
oi.line: Hokusai’s daughter. About ten works confirmed as hers. Her hand is inside work signed “Hokusai” (probable).
oi.bet: That a hand could work for years inside a famous man’s name.

highlights.t: About ten works confirmed as hers
Painted in her father’s studio
Her hand in work signed “Hokusai”

oi.story:
Katsushika Ōi was Hokusai’s daughter. Her dates are uncertain: she was born around 1800 and is last recorded in the 1850s (probable).
She worked as a painter in her father’s studio for most of her life. Only about ten works are confirmed as hers, among them the *Night Scene in the Yoshiwara*, with its lantern light and deep shadow.
Hokusai “is reported to have said” that her pictures of women were better than his.
Orders sent to “Hokusai” could be painted by father or daughter and signed with his name (probable).
That makes her the clearest case in this story of a hand hidden by the trade’s naming rules. One historian argues that her hand was made to vanish, “for profit”.
No reliable likeness of her survives, so her card carries her art name in a seal frame. The Ōta Memorial Museum showed her night scene in 2023.

eisen.name: Keisai Eisen
eisen.line: His all-blue fan of 1829 started the fad. Van Gogh copied one of his courtesans.
eisen.bet: That one imported colour, in gradations, was enough.

highlights.t: His all-blue fan of 1829 started the fad
Began the Kisokaidō series that Hiroshige finished
Van Gogh copied one of his courtesans

eisen.story:
Keisai Eisen was born in Edo in 1790, the son of a noted calligrapher of the Ikeda family. He trained with the Kanō painter Hakkeisai, who gave him the name Keisai, and then with Kikukawa Eizan.
He is best known for *bijin-ga*, pictures of beautiful women, drawn as more worldly than earlier designers had drawn them.
In 1829 the fan-maker Iseya Sōbei put out his fan printed in shades of Prussian blue alone. By Tōho’s account it was a sensation. The fad that followed carried Hokusai’s Fuji series.
Later he designed the first eleven sheets of the *Sixty-nine Stations of the Kisokaidō*, before Hiroshige took the series over.
He also wrote, including lives of the forty-seven rōnin and a history of the floating-world prints. He drew the portrait of Hokusai on Hokusai’s card.
He died in 1848. In 1887 Van Gogh copied one of his courtesans in oil.

hiroshige.name: Utagawa Hiroshige
hiroshige.cap: Utagawa Kunisada, memorial portrait of Hiroshige, 1858 · The Met, CC0
hiroshige.line: The Tōkaidō of 1833–34. The Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1856–58.
hiroshige.bet: That travellers and townspeople would buy the places they knew.

highlights.t: Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō, 1833–34
One Hundred Famous Views of Edo, 1856–58
More than 8,000 works

hiroshige.story:
Utagawa Hiroshige was born Andō Tokutarō in Edo in 1797. His father was a fire warden for the Yayosu quay.
He studied under Utagawa Toyohiro. His breakthrough was the *Fifty-three Stations of the Tōkaidō*, published by Hōeidō in 1833–34: fifty-five sheets of the road from Nihonbashi to Kyoto.
Series of famous places followed, for Osaka in 1834, Lake Biwa in 1834 and Kyoto in 1835. He finished the *Sixty-nine Stations of the Kisokaidō*, begun by Keisai Eisen.
His last great project was the *One Hundred Famous Views of Edo* for the publisher Uoya Eikichi, 1856–58. Its 118 sheets show the city from spots you could walk to.
He died in 1858, aged 62, during an epidemic of cholera in Edo; whether it killed him is unknown. He left more than eight thousand works. In 1887 Van Gogh copied two.

kuniyoshi.name: Utagawa Kuniyoshi
kuniyoshi.cap: Utagawa Yoshiiku, memorial portrait of Kuniyoshi, 1861 · British Museum via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
kuniyoshi.line: Warriors from 1827, cats always. 408,000 sheets of loyal retainers in eight months.
kuniyoshi.bet: That warriors, cats and ghosts could say what actors no longer could.

highlights.t: Breakthrough with the Suikoden heroes, 1827
408,000 sheets of loyal retainers, 1847–48
Cats in place of people in comic prints

kuniyoshi.story:
Utagawa Kuniyoshi was born on 1 January 1798, the son of a silk-dyer. At about twelve his drawing caught the eye of the designer Utagawa Toyokuni, who took him on.
His breakthrough came in 1827 with a series of heroes from the popular *Suikoden*. Warriors became his genre.
The Tenpō reforms banned actors and courtesans from single sheets. Kuniyoshi made the most of what was left. He drew cats in the place of people, ghosts and monsters, and comic pictures that disguised real actors.
Some were read as criticism of the shogunate, such as an 1843 design of a sleeping warrior haunted by demons.
In 1847 his fifty-one loyal retainers sold eight thousand sets, 408,000 sheets, by the Fujiokaya diary’s count.
He died at home in Genyadana in April 1861, aged 63.

kunisada.cap: Toyohara Kunichika, memorial portrait of Kunisada · Brooklyn Museum via Wikimedia Commons · public domain

egawa.line: Carver. In 1835 Hokusai gave up his own share of the carving fee to secure him.

kido.line: Carver, named in the Smithsonian’s 1889 Tokunō gift.

yamamoto.line: Printer of the Nandina proofs in the Tokunō gift, 1889.

sadanobu.name: Matsudaira Sadanobu
sadanobu.line: Chief councillor 1787–93. His reforms put a censor’s seal on every print.
sadanobu.bet: That a frugal, moral city could be ordered by law.

highlights.t: Chief senior councillor, 1787–1793
Kansei reforms: austerity and sumptuary laws
Every print to carry a censor’s seal from 1790

sadanobu.story:
Matsudaira Sadanobu was born on 15 January 1759, a grandson of the reforming eighth shogun, Tokugawa Yoshimune. He became daimyō of Shirakawa, in the north.
He took charge after the great Tenmei famine of 1782–88. As chief senior councillor from 1787 to 1793 he led the Kansei reforms: austerity, sumptuary laws and rural reconstruction, meant to prevent another uprising.
For the print trade the reforms meant censorship. From 1790 every design went to censors chosen from the publishers’ own guild, and approved sheets carried the *kiwame* seal.
In 1791 the writer Kyōden was manacled and his publisher Tsutaya fined half his property.
Sadanobu was also a writer and a moralist, under the pen name Rakuō. The portrait on his card is his own, painted in 1787. He died on 14 June 1829.

tadakuni.bet: That banning the city’s pleasures would restore its discipline.

highlights.t: Led the Tenpō reforms, 1841–43
Actors, courtesans and geisha banned from single sheets, 1842
A sheet capped at 16 mon

tadakuni.story:
Mizuno Tadakuni was born on 19 July 1794. He was daimyō of Karatsu and then of Hamamatsu, and rose to the shogunate’s council of elders.
He took charge after the great Tenpō famine of 1832–36. His reforms tried to restore the frugality, simplicity and discipline of the early Edo period, banning most entertainment and displays of wealth.
For the print trade, 1842 was the year of the order. In the sixth month single sheets of actors, courtesans and geisha were banned. In the eleventh, sheets and fan prints were capped at sixteen mon. The three theatres were moved to Saruwaka-chō.
A land order, the *Agechi-rei*, asked lords near Edo and Osaka to give up their holdings, and proved unpopular (probable). He was relieved of office in February 1845 and died on 12 March 1851.

tokuno.name: Tokunō Michimasa
tokuno.line: Head of the government Printing Bureau. Sent the Smithsonian a complete printing set in 1889.
tokuno.bet: That the state could show the world how a print was made.

highlights.t: Sent the Smithsonian a complete printing set, 1889
More than a hundred progressive proofs
Its records name the carver and the printers

tokuno.story:
Tokunō Michimasa headed Japan’s government Printing Bureau in the 1880s. The bureau printed the state’s own paper: stamps, bonds and banknotes (probable).
In 1889 he sent the Smithsonian Institution in Washington a complete set for making a colour woodblock print. It held the carved blocks, the tools, the pigments and more than a hundred progressive proofs, each showing one more colour laid down.
The gift’s records did something the Edo trade almost never did. They named the makers: the carver Kido Kotarō, and the printers Yamamoto Iwakichi and Nakamura Tsurusaburō, with Morikawa Kokichirō recorded for one sheet.
So the carvers and printers of this story get their names once, in a state’s gift to a foreign museum. The proofs are educational-use only, so this unit links to them.
The bureau’s successor, the National Printing Bureau, prints the thousand-yen note with the Great Wave today (probable).

kyoden.bet: That a comic book could sell like a print, ten thousand copies at a time.

highlights.t: Designed as Kitao Masanobu, wrote as Kyōden
Handcuffed fifty days for three books, 1791
Ran a tobacco shop in Ginza from 1793

kyoden.story:
Santō Kyōden was born in Fukagawa, Edo, on 13 September 1761. He trained as a designer under Kitao Shigemasa and illustrated comic books as Kitao Masanobu.
He then wrote his own: *kibyōshi*, satirical picture books, and *sharebon*, stories of the pleasure quarter. In the 1790s one of his books could sell ten thousand copies.
In 1791 three of his *sharebon*, published by Tsutaya, were judged offensive under the Kansei reforms. He was handcuffed for fifty days.
He changed course. From the autumn of 1793 he ran a successful tobacco shop in Ginza, and advertised it in his own books. He turned to *yomihon*, longer and more moral books for reading.
He died in 1816. His caricature of Tsutaya, drawn in 1791, is the publisher’s best-known likeness, and it is on Tsutaya’s card.

hayashi.name: Hayashi Tadamasa
hayashi.line: Paris dealer from 1884. 218 shipments of prints and books in eleven years.
hayashi.bet: That Paris would buy Japan’s cheap sheets as art, if a Japanese chose them.

highlights.t: Came to Paris for the 1878 exposition
218 shipments from Japan in eleven years
166,000 prints, or more than 300,000 works

hayashi.story:
Hayashi Tadamasa was born in 1853. He came to Paris as an interpreter for the Exposition universelle of 1878, and stayed.
In 1884 he opened his own shop. Over the next eleven years he made 218 shipments from Japan.
One study counts 166,000 prints and 9,708 illustrated books among them. Another estimate says more than 300,000 works (argued).
That makes him the second trade’s central figure. A Japanese dealer chose much of what Paris saw, priced it, and sold it to collectors and painters.
The great Paris collections of Japanese prints were built in large part from his crates (probable).
The argument over Japonisme, exchange or appropriation, turns on dealers like him, who were Japanese and made the selection.
He died in 1906. In 2019 the National Museum of Western Art in Tokyo gave him an exhibition of his own.

bing.name: Siegfried Bing
bing.cap: Photograph before 1906 · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
bing.line: Le Japon artistique, 1888–91. Over 700 prints at the École des Beaux-Arts in 1890.
bing.bet: That Japanese design could change European art, with a magazine to show it.

highlights.t: Le Japon artistique, 1888–91
Over 700 prints at the École des Beaux-Arts, 1890
Opened the Maison de l’Art Nouveau, 1895

bing.story:
Siegfried Bing was born in Hamburg on 26 February 1838 and moved to France in 1854. He usually signed himself S. Bing.
He became one of the Paris dealers who brought Japanese art to Europe, and he travelled to Japan himself.
From 1888 he published *Le Japon artistique*, a monthly journal in French, English and German, collected in three volumes in 1891. It put Japanese prints, textiles and objects in front of designers across Europe.
In 1890 he hung over seven hundred prints at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris. The painters came to look.
In December 1895 he opened a new gallery, the Maison de l’Art Nouveau. Its name became the name of a style.
He died on 6 September 1905.

vangogh.name: Vincent van Gogh
vangogh.cap: Self-Portrait, 1887 · Art Institute of Chicago via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
vangogh.line: Bought about 660 prints in early 1887. Painted three copies that autumn.
vangogh.bet: That cheap Japanese prints could teach a European painter to see colour.

highlights.t: Bought about 660 Japanese prints, early 1887
Painted three copies in oil that autumn
Two after Hiroshige, one after Eisen

vangogh.story:
Vincent van Gogh met Japanese prints as a buyer. In early 1887, in Paris, he bought about 660 of them: cheap sheets from the second trade, probably from Bing’s stock (probable).
He hung some in a Paris café and studied the rest closely.
That autumn he painted three copies in oil. Two were after Hiroshige’s *Hundred Famous Views of Edo*: the plum orchard at Kameido and the sudden shower over Shin-Ōhashi. The third copied a courtesan by Keisai Eisen.
His copies change what they copy. The colours are heightened, and he painted borders of Japanese characters around them (probable).
Both Hiroshige sheets were published by Uoya Eikichi, and both carry their censor’s seals.
The copies and many of the prints are in the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam. The museum’s licence is non-commercial, so this unit links to them and does not show them.
vangogh.worksNote: The sheets he copied, by Hiroshige and Eisen; his own copies are linked, not shown.

fenollosa.name: Ernest Fenollosa
fenollosa.cap: Photograph, c. 1890 · Wikimedia Commons · public domain
fenollosa.line: Boston’s curator of Oriental art from 1890. Curated the earliest known ukiyo-e exhibition in Japan, Tokyo, 1898.
fenollosa.bet: That Japan’s own art needed saving, and that the prints belonged in its history.

highlights.t: Taught at the Imperial University, Tokyo, from 1878
Curator of Oriental art, Boston, 1890
Curated the earliest known ukiyo-e show in Japan, 1898

fenollosa.story:
Ernest Fenollosa was born in Salem, Massachusetts, on 18 February 1853. In 1878 he was invited to Japan, and taught political economy and philosophy at the Imperial University in Tokyo.
He became a champion of traditional Japanese art, then out of favour in a modernising country (probable). After eight years at the university he helped found the Tokyo School of Fine Arts and the Tokyo Imperial Museum.
He converted to Buddhism and took the name Teishin.
In 1890 he returned to Boston as curator of the Museum of Fine Arts’ department of Oriental art. In 1896 he published *Masters of Ukiyoe*, for an exhibition in New York.
In 1898 he curated an exhibition of ukiyo-e in Tokyo, the earliest known in Japan.
He died in London in 1908. His ashes were buried at Mii-dera, by Lake Biwa.

wright.name: Frank Lloyd Wright
wright.cap: Photograph, 1926 · Library of Congress via Wikimedia Commons · public domain
wright.line: Architect and print dealer. A Hiroshige show in Chicago, 1906; a scandal, 1920.
wright.bet: That Japanese prints were a lesson in design, and a business.

highlights.t: Lent the Art Institute a Hiroshige exhibition, 1906
A Spaulding commission grew to $125,000 in 1913
Refunded about $30,000 after the “revamped” prints

wright.story:
Frank Lloyd Wright went to Japan in 1905 and came back a collector. In 1906 he lent the Art Institute of Chicago a whole exhibition of Hiroshige prints.
For about twenty years he also dealt in them. In 1913 a commission from the Boston collectors William and John Spaulding grew from twenty thousand dollars to 125,000 in five months.
A *Plum Garden at Kameido* in Chicago records him as the seller to Kate Buckingham, in February 1915.
In 1919–20 some prints he had sold proved “revamped”: faded impressions recut and recoloured. The fraud was traced to a Tokyo dealer and a collector. Wright refunded about thirty thousand dollars.
In 1928 his bank seized his house, and thousands of his prints sold at a dollar each.
The Hammer Museum’s exhibition of 2005 traced what the prints taught his architecture.
